newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Emergency rule clamped on crisis-torn Ecuador.
newsitem.headline: Emergency rule clamped on crisis-torn Ecuador.

text.p: A state of emergency was declared in Ecuador on Friday as fresh street protests and general mayhem gripped the nation a day after Congress voted to oust President Abdala Bucaram for mental incompetence.
Defence Minister Victor Bayas announced the state of emergency, which suspends the right to stage public demonstrations and other individual guarantees, in a terse statement on national television.
"I believe it is necessary to declare a state of national emergency to preserve the country's peace," he said.

His statement came shortly after hundreds of riot police fired tear gas into a crowd of about 5,000 demonstrators in Quito's colonial city centre to prevent them from marching on Independence Square, just outside the ornate Carondelet presidential palace.

Bucaram, known as "El Loco" or "madman," has been holed up inside the palace since his ouster by Congress on Thursday night, a move that he described as an act of "judicial barbarity" and a de facto coup.
Bucaram, in remarks to reporters on Friday, reiterated his earlier pledges to defy the vote removing him from office, saying he intended to see out his full term of office.

But Bucaram -- who appeared to be clinging to power by little more than a thread -- opened the door to a possible solution of the country's worst political crisis by saying he was prepared to submit himself to a "political trial" in Congress if it would help restore confidence in his six-month-old government.
"If anyone is interested in questioning (my) rule all the channels are open for a political trial," he said.

Bucaram was summarily ousted after a two-day strike shut down the country in protest against a tough economic austerity plan he unveiled early last month. His detractors accused him not only of incompetence but of runaway levels of corruption since he took office.
With or without a trial, many Ecuadoreans said they expected the military to assume a role as the final arbiter of power in the tiny South American country.

In Washington, the United States said it was concerned by the constitutional crisis in Ecuador and the State Department urged the political leadership in Quito to resolve its disputes peacefully and within the bounds of Ecuadorean laws.
"The continuation of this climate of uncertainty can only damage Ecuador's national interests and its standing in the community of democratic nations," it added.
Fabian Alarcon, the congressional leader sworn in by his fellow lawmakers to replace Bucaram as interim head of state, was among those who saw the military's role as crucial.
In a statement early on Friday, he urged military leaders to join civilians in a march through the capital and demand that Bucaram step down immediately.
"We have absolutely nothing to negotiate with ... Bucaram, the former president, or with Mrs. Rosalia Arteaga, the vice president," Alarcon said.
Arteaga, who pundits say has no political power base, has also staked a claim to the presidency, insisting she was next in line to succeed the sitting president.
The constitution is extemely vague on the whole issue of successions, however, and Alarcon is seen as far more likely to occupy the presidential palace -- should Bucaram ever decide to move out.

Hinting that it was not prepared to remain on the sidelines for long, the military issued a statement at a pre-dawn news conference on Friday urging a speedy end to the worst political crisis in Ecuador's 167-year history as an independent state.
It said the military, which ruled Ecuador for seven years until 1979, was prepared to mediate in the crisis in a bid to end political infighting and squabbling between Arteaga and Alarcon.
